summary: Supply the price per weight unit, the spread and the bid price and the Scrap silver calculator solves for pure silver weight. Think of it as a shortcut for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Scrap silver calculator work?
sections.html:
The Scrap silver calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports pure silver weight in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the silver purity); then you type in the price per weight unit, the spread and the bid price (sell).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Scrap silver calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Pure silver weight=silver value ÷ price per weight unit
Weight of scrap silver=pure silver weight ÷ silver purity
Ask price (buy)=silver value × (spread + 1)
Silver value=-bid price (sell) ÷ (spread − 1)
Custom purity=silver purity

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Open the page and it is already filled in. With the values it starts from — Silver purity set to .999 - fine, Price per weight unit = 19 and Spread = 5 % — it reports Custom purity = 99.9 ‰.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Custom purity = 99.9 ‰ should be roughly the size you expected from Silver purity set to .999 - fine and Price per weight unit = 19.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Mass, opening in troy ounces

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Scrap silver calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the price per weight unit, the spread and the bid price — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Scrap silver calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns pure silver weight, derived from the price per weight unit, the spread and the bid price. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Scrap silver calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the price per weight unit, the spread and the bid price, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter weight of scrap silver in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Weight of scrap silver opens in troy ounces and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Custom purity = 99.9 ‰. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Scrap silver calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
